---
title: "A Qubit Is a Probability-Amplitude State"
description: "A rigorous introductory lesson with one small example, mathematical notation and a proof-oriented explanation."
---

## Start with an ordinary situation

A classical bit is either 0 or 1. A qubit can be in a state whose measurement sometimes produces 0 and sometimes 1. It is not a little coin storing both readable answers at once.

## The core concept

A pure one-qubit state is a complex vector with two amplitudes. Measurement probabilities come from squared magnitudes, not the amplitudes themselves.

## Express it mathematically

$$
|\psi\rangle=\alpha|0\rangle+\beta|1\rangle,\qquad |\alpha|^2+|\beta|^2=1
$$

**Every symbol explained:** |ψ⟩ is the qubit state; |0⟩ and |1⟩ are basis states; α and β are complex amplitudes; absolute-value-squared is the magnitude squared. The right equation enforces total measurement probability one.

**Substitute actual numbers:** Choose α=√3/2 and β=1/2. Then P(0)=|√3/2|²=3/4=75%, P(1)=|1/2|²=1/4=25%; they add to 100%. One measurement returns a single classical outcome, not both.

## Why it works

The state is a vector in a two-dimensional complex Hilbert space. A computational-basis measurement returns one basis value with probability determined by the squared amplitude.

## Go one level deeper

Measurement probabilities depend on the measurement basis. Global phase cannot be directly observed; relative phase matters in interference.

## Common misunderstanding

Do not claim that a qubit stores an arbitrary amount of classical information accessible in one measurement.

## Check your understanding

Explain the example with different numbers. Identify which assumption makes the derivation work, and which assumption would invalidate it. Then write the mathematical model again without looking.
